title: Coriolanus Turned Back by His Mother
text:
Gnaeus Marcius, called Coriolanus for his courage at the capture of Corioli, was driven out of Rome by the people he had scorned. According to the tradition preserved by Livy and Plutarch, he went over to the Volscians, Rome's enemies, and led their army to within a few miles of the city. Rome sent envoys, then priests. He sent them all away.

Then the women of Rome went out to his camp. At their head walked his aged mother, with his wife and his small sons. Livy calls the mother Veturia and the wife Volumnia; Plutarch gives the mother the name Volumnia. Coriolanus rushed to embrace his mother, but she stopped him and asked whether she had come to an enemy or to a son, and whether she was a captive in his camp. She told him that if she had never borne a son, Rome would not now be under attack.

The man who had refused every embassy broke down. Plutarch records his answer: "O mother, what have you done to me?" He said she had won a victory that saved Rome and ruined her son. He withdrew the Volscian army. The traditions disagree on his end: some say the Volscians killed him, others that he lived on in exile. Rome, Livy says, built a temple to Fortuna Muliebris, the Fortune of Women, in memory of the day.
lesson: The people who raised us often reach us when no argument can. When someone is set on a destructive course, the voice that matters may be the one closest to home.
source: Livy, History of Rome 2.39 to 2.40; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 33 to 36
caveat: The story belongs to Rome's early legendary history, and even the names of the women differ between Livy and Plutarch.
